title: The Spotify Student: Reckoning with Audiobooks
author: Jeannette DeCelles-Zwerneman
summary: Jeannette DeCelles-Zwerneman, writing for the classical education pedagogy newsletter, argues that the rising classroom reliance on audiobooks is quietly deepening America's literacy crisis rather than solving it. She opens with NAEP data showing that reading proficiency has been declining since the 1990s, well before COVID school closures, and describes professors reporting that students can no longer sustain attention through a full novel or long-form argument. Her central claim is that listening to an audiobook is structurally similar to reading a commentary: someone else has already made the interpretive decisions, so the student absorbs a performance of the text rather than doing the work of reading it. She illustrates the kind of active, puzzling engagement she wants to preserve with worked examples from classical and modern texts, showing how a real reader stops, rereads, and reconstructs an argument's logic. The piece closes with a direct appeal to teachers to resist audiobooks as a shortcut and instead train students toward genuine reading proficiency, since interpretation and discovery, not merely hearing words, are what make someone a reader.
points: The 2024 NAEP data shows reading proficiency began declining in the 1990s, not with COVID school closures, undercutting the common assumption that the pandemic alone explains the literacy crisis.

DeCelles-Zwerneman argues audiobooks function like reading commentaries: they outsource the interpretive work of reading to someone else, so students absorb a performance without doing the cognitive labor that makes them readers.
High school teachers report that heavy audiobook use leaves students unable to locate key passages or track plot, character, and word choice, the very skills close reading is meant to build.
The piece frames independent slow reading as the precondition for the moment of a student discovering meaning for themselves, and treats audiobooks as a structural threat to that discovery.
Her prescription is practical: train younger students toward reading proficiency and reserve audiobooks as a last resort, not a default classroom accommodation.
quotes: Both the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress report (commonly referred to as the Nation's Report Card) and the Manhattan Institute's thorough analysis of that report indicate that the decline in literacy predates the pandemic.

The audiobook reader has already made the critically important interpretive decisions for the listener, thus preempting the most important objective of any humanities course: that is, to train students in careful, close, interpretative reading skills. The students do not actually have to read at all when using audiobooks.

High school teachers on the ground confess that the majority of their students are employing audiobooks. As a result, the students have difficulty locating key passages in the text; understanding important developments in plot, character, and the use of words; and recognizing the beauty and elegance of the writing.

Puzzling over a passage, worrying over it, teasing out its implications, relishing its beauty, craft, and humor—these are the activities of a thoughtful, active mind at work when reading an important piece of literature. Reading is discovering a word that delights the mind or a logical move that brings pleasure and new understanding.
Reading is about more than seeing words on the page or even reading those words. It is the student's interpretation and discovery of meaning that makes that student a reader.
When I first began teaching, our students made a firm commitment not to consult commentaries of any kind when studying great works of literature. It was even a written policy in our student handbook.
